newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Indian bond market reforms a key step - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Indian bond market reforms a key step - analysts.

text.p: India's move to open its domestic bond market to foreign investors is a key step to financial market reform, analysts said on Thursday.

"I think it is a substantial step in that it is the first time the government has had the confidence to allow foreigners to take up Indian debt," said Raja Visweswaran, head of fixed income research at Bank of America Securities in Hong Kong.
"I think it also signals the government's determination to go ahead with the economics reform programme," he said on Reuters Financial Television's (RFTV) weekly Asian Debt Briefing.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) said earlier this year that foreign investors would be allowed to invest in government securities for the first time.
Pratip Kar, SEBI executive director, said two foreign bond funds, in addition to the three already chosen, will soon be approved to invest in gilts and corporate bonds.
The three that have been named are J. Henry Schroeder, Credit Suisse and Chescor.
"So far, we have cleared five funds with a total of some US$500 million to invest," Kar told reporters in Hong Kong.

Foreign funds can invest in longer-dated government securities but not in bills, which have maturities of less than one year. The restriction is designed to limit short-term capital inflows, Kar said.
Kar and other Indian regulatory officials were in Hong Kong as part of an Asian roadshow to explain India's reforms to institutional investors in the region.
The roadshow, sponsored by Merrill Lynch, began in Tokyo and will continue to Singapore on Friday.
SEBI chairman D.R. Mehta highlighted for investors in Hong Kong the improvements in India's equity and capital markets that have made them more liquid and transparent.
He said India was committed to reforming financial markets and improvements will continue.
Dalip Awasthi, executive director of UBS in Singapore, told RFTV he expects foreign investors will be enticed by the high yields of rupee-denominated debt, which are in the "mid to high teens."

Even if the rupee depreciates by four to six percent against the dollar in the future, "you are still getting close to 250 to 300 basis points over U.S. Treasuries," he said. He added that Indian dollar debt offered in the Eurobond market offers signficantly less than that.

Indian institutions are tapping the international bond markets again after a respite. Industrial Credit and Investment Corp of India (ICICI) and Industrial Bank of India (IDBI) will launch Eurobonds this month.
Bankers said Indian issuers would have an easier time accessing international capital markets if India were to launch a benchmark sovereign bond.

Samir Shah, vice president, Asia-Pacific Capital Markets at Salomon Brothers, told RFTV that a benchmark issue would help foreign investors assess Indian corporate credits relative to the perceived risk of the sovereign paper.

L.K. Narayan, vice president of origination at Merrill Lynch in Bombay, said India would likely postpone a sovereign bond until it is rated investment grade by both Moody's Investors Service and Standard and Poor's Corp.
Moody's rates India investment grade at Baa3, while S&P assesses the country at BB-plus, a notch below investment grade.

Speaking at the Merrill conference, Narendra Jadhav, officer-in-charge in the Reserve Bank of India's Department of Economics, said India currently has no plans to launch a sovereign bond but may in the future as the country's external balances improve.
